causal_claim: Daniel Bernoulli's logarithmic utility made cross-entropy loss possible by first scoring outcomes with a logarithm weighted by probability, the log-probability form cross-entropy averages.
definition: Bernoulli proposed valuing uncertain outcomes by expected logarithmic utility, log(w), rather than expected money, in his 1738 St. Petersburg paper.
name: Daniel Bernoulli's logarithmic utility (1738)
source_title: The St. Petersburg Paradox - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

causal_claim: Bayes' theorem made cross-entropy loss possible by defining the posterior distribution that a predicted distribution must be scored against.
definition: Bayes' posthumous 1763 essay gives a rule for inverting conditional probabilities to obtain a posterior distribution over an unknown parameter from observed successes and failures.
name: Bayes' theorem (1763)

causal_claim: Legendre's method of least squares made cross-entropy loss possible by establishing the template of training by minimizing a principled scalar loss over data, which cross-entropy later replaced for distributions.
definition: Legendre published in 1805 a fitting procedure that chooses parameters minimizing the sum of squared errors between model and observations.
name: Legendre's method of least squares (1805)

causal_claim: Pearson's chi-squared test made cross-entropy loss possible by giving an explicit, category-by-category score of how far an observed distribution departs from an expected one.
definition: Pearson's 1900 test quantifies distributional mismatch as the sum over categories of (observed-expected)^2/expected and tests goodness of fit.
name: Pearson's chi-squared test (1900)

causal_claim: Fisher's maximum likelihood estimation made cross-entropy loss possible by showing training is maximizing log-likelihood, which is exactly minimizing cross-entropy against the empirical distribution.
definition: Fisher's 1922 paper formalized choosing parameters that maximize the likelihood, in practice its logarithm, of the observed data under the model.
name: Fisher's maximum likelihood estimation (1922)

causal_claim: Napier's logarithms made cross-entropy loss possible by supplying the logarithm, the function whose negative expectation over one distribution under another is cross-entropy.
definition: Napier published logarithms in Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio (1614), turning multiplication into addition via precomputed tables.
name: Napier's logarithms (1614)

causal_claim: Huygens's expectation made cross-entropy loss possible by supplying the expectation operator under the true distribution that cross-entropy is defined as, E_p[-log q].
definition: Huygens's De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (1657), the first printed probability textbook, formalized expectation as the probability-weighted value of an uncertain prospect.
name: Huygens's expectation (1657)
source_title: Huygens - De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (Dartmouth)

causal_claim: Bernoulli's law of large numbers made cross-entropy loss possible by guaranteeing an empirical distribution converges to the true distribution that cross-entropy scores predictions against.
definition: Jacob Bernoulli's posthumous Ars Conjectandi (1713) proved the law of large numbers, that observed frequencies converge to the true probability.
name: Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi and law of large numbers (1713)
source_title: Bernoulli's Law of Large Numbers - Cambridge / ASTIN Bulletin

causal_claim: De Moivre's normal approximation made cross-entropy loss possible by giving a concrete parametric probability distribution family whose likelihood could be scored and optimized.
definition: In 1733 De Moivre approximated the binomial distribution by the bell-shaped normal curve, the first explicit continuous probability distribution of that form.
name: De Moivre's normal approximation to the binomial (1733)
source_title: Normal approximation to the Binomial - Yale Statistics

causal_claim: Gauss's normal error law made cross-entropy loss possible by linking a distribution, its log-density and maximum likelihood, the derivation pattern later used for classifier losses.
definition: Gauss's Theoria Motus (1809) derived the normal distribution as the error law that makes the arithmetic mean the most probable value and justifies least squares.
name: Gauss's normal error law (1809)

causal_claim: Clausius's entropy made cross-entropy loss possible by creating the named, quantified entropy concept that Shannon entropy and cross-entropy mathematically generalize.
definition: Clausius in 1865 gave entropy its name and mathematical form dS = dQ_rev/T as a state function measuring transformation content.
name: Clausius's entropy (1865)

causal_claim: Maxwell's velocity distribution made cross-entropy loss possible by showing a physical system is described by a probability distribution over states, the object cross-entropy compares.
definition: Maxwell derived in 1860 the probability distribution of molecular speeds in a gas, the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
name: Maxwell's velocity distribution (1860)

causal_claim: Boltzmann's entropy formula made cross-entropy loss possible by first writing entropy as a logarithm of a probability, the -sum p log p structure cross-entropy extends to two distributions.
definition: Boltzmann in 1877 defined entropy as S = k log W, the logarithm of the number of microstates corresponding to a macrostate.
name: Boltzmann's entropy formula (1877)

causal_claim: Gibbs's statistical mechanics made cross-entropy loss possible by expressing entropy as an expectation of log-probability over an ensemble distribution, one step from cross-entropy's expectation under a different distribution.
definition: Gibbs's Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902) systematized ensembles, with entropy as the negative average index of probability, -sum p log p in modern form.
name: Gibbs's statistical mechanics and Gibbs entropy (1902)
source_title: Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics - Project Gutenberg

causal_claim: Hartley's logarithmic measure made cross-entropy loss possible by defining information as a logarithm of possibilities, the direct precursor Shannon weighted by probabilities to get entropy and cross-entropy.
definition: Hartley's 1928 Transmission of Information quantified information as H = log S^n = n log S, the logarithm of the number of possible symbol sequences.
name: Hartley's logarithmic measure of information (1928)

causal_claim: Briggs's Arithmetica Logarithmica made cross-entropy loss possible by making logarithms a cheap table lookup, so log-probability scores could actually be computed by hand.
definition: Briggs published in 1624 tables of common base-10 logarithms of 30,000 numbers to fourteen decimal places.
name: Briggs's Arithmetica Logarithmica (1624)

causal_claim: Oughtred's slide rule made cross-entropy loss possible by embodying logarithms in a physical instrument that added log lengths, mechanizing the arithmetic a log-loss requires.
definition: Oughtred invented the slide rule about 1622 by sliding two logarithmic Gunter scales against each other to multiply and divide directly.
name: Oughtred's slide rule (1622)

causal_claim: The Pascaline made cross-entropy loss possible by proving repeated arithmetic over many numbers could be mechanized, a precondition for summing log-losses over datasets.
definition: Pascal's Pascaline, invented in 1642, was a mechanical calculator that added and subtracted with an automatic carry mechanism.
name: Pascaline mechanical calculator (1642)

causal_claim: Babbage's Difference Engine made cross-entropy loss possible by pursuing error-free automated table computation, the calculation infrastructure needed to evaluate losses at scale.
definition: Babbage announced the Difference Engine in 1822 to automate computation and printing of mathematical tables, especially logarithm tables for navigation.
name: Babbage's Difference Engine (1822)

causal_claim: The Hollerith tabulating machine made cross-entropy loss possible by mechanizing counting of categorical outcomes into frequency distributions, the empirical distributions cross-entropy is computed from.
definition: Hollerith's electromechanical punched-card tabulator processed the 1890 US census, counting cards by category far faster than hand tabulation.
name: Hollerith tabulating machine (1890)
source_title: The Hollerith Machine - US Census Bureau

causal_claim: Kepler's Rudolphine Tables made cross-entropy loss possible by showing printed tables of predicted positions could be checked against observed reality, the prediction-versus-reality substrate of a loss.
definition: Kepler's Rudolphine Tables (1627), built on Tycho Brahe's observations, gave planetary positions and included logarithm tables for their computation.
name: Kepler's Rudolphine Tables (1627)
source_title: Kepler and Astronomical Tables - Cambridge HPS

causal_claim: Graunt's Observations made cross-entropy loss possible by first turning raw counts into an empirical probability distribution over outcomes, the target distribution in cross-entropy.
definition: Graunt's 1662 analysis of London's Bills of Mortality produced the first life table, turning parish death records into survival proportions.
name: Graunt's Observations on the Bills of Mortality (1662)
source_title: Graunt's Life Table - Institute and Faculty of Actuaries

causal_claim: Halley's Breslau life table made cross-entropy loss possible by providing a complete age-by-age empirical distribution used for probabilistic pricing, a concrete model of scoring predictions from a distribution.
definition: Halley published in 1693 a life table from Breslau birth and death records for 1687-1691 and used it to price life annuities by age.
name: Halley's Breslau life table (1693)
source_title: A new look at Halley's life table - JRSS A (Bellhouse)

causal_claim: The Nautical Almanac made cross-entropy loss possible by institutionalizing large-scale printed predicted-versus-observed tables and duplicate computation to check them, making distributional prediction a routine practice.
definition: Maskelyne's Nautical Almanac, first issued for 1767, published lunar-distance and astronomical tables computed in duplicate by human computers for navigation.
name: The Nautical Almanac (1767)
source_title: The Nautical Almanac and associated publications - Royal Observatory Greenwich

causal_claim: Quetelet's Sur l'homme made cross-entropy loss possible by showing whole populations form concrete normal distributions in printed data, extending distributional thinking from errors to real categorical and measured populations.
definition: Quetelet's Sur l'homme (1835) applied the normal distribution to measured human traits in large populations, centred on the homme moyen or average man.
name: Quetelet's Sur l'homme and the average man (1835)
